title: Stashing Work & Release Tagging
description: Shelve unfinished changes temporarily with git stash and mark milestone releases with lightweight and annotated tags.

blocks.content: Sometimes you're in the middle of something and need to switch to a different task urgently. You can't commit half-finished work, but you also don't want to lose it. That's what **stashing** is for. A stash temporarily tucks your changes away so you can come back to them later.

## Stashing Changes

Save all uncommitted changes to the stash:
```
git stash
```

Give it a name so you remember what it was:
```
git stash push -m "half-done login form"
```

Your working directory is now clean (back to the last commit). Fix the urgent thing, then bring your stashed work back:
```
git stash pop
```

See what's in your stash:
```
git stash list
```

## Tagging Releases

A **tag** is a permanent, human-readable label on a specific commit. Unlike branches (which move as you commit), tags never move. They're used to mark release versions.

Create a tag on the current commit:
```
git tag v1.0.0
```

Push a tag to a remote (tags aren't pushed automatically):
```
git push origin v1.0.0
```

List all tags:
```
git tag
```

blocks.question: You're halfway through a feature when your boss asks you to fix a critical bug right now. What should you do with your unfinished work?
options: Delete the changes and start fresh after the fix
Commit the half-finished code with a note
Stash the changes, fix the bug, then pop the stash to continue
Open a second terminal window and work in both
blocks.explanation: `git stash` saves your unfinished changes to a safe temporary area, leaving your working directory clean. You can switch branches, fix the bug, commit it, then `git stash pop` to restore your previous work exactly as you left it.
